name: Oregano (Origanum)
short: Case report: INR 6.42 (bleeding risk) on acenocoumarol with oregano and verbena tea. Allergy cases: systemic reactions to eaten oregano and thyme; child angioedema. Oil: skin irritation (title only).
text: Anticoagulant interaction (case report): a 2025 report describes a 77-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation whose INR had been stable in the target range of 2 to 3 for 4 years on acenocoumarol, a vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant. At a routine check her INR was 6.42; she had started drinking an infusion (tea) of oregano (Origanum vulgare), and occasionally verbena, daily for a week. Her INR fell to 3.80 the next day after the anticoagulant was paused and returned to range after she stopped the tea; when, despite being told of the risk, she went back to drinking oregano tea from her garden, her INR was stabilised after changes to both her tea and her anticoagulant treatment were recommended. The abstract does not report any bleeding. The authors attribute the rise to an interaction that they say increases bleeding risk, propose that oregano and verbena polyphenols inhibit the liver enzymes CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 and that oregano's carvacrol and thymol have anticoagulant activity, and say the interaction with acenocoumarol deserves to be recognised and monitored; because verbena was also taken, the case cannot show which plant was responsible. Allergy: a case report describes a 13-year-old boy with allergy to three plants of the mint family (sage, peppermint and Origanum onites, a species of oregano) who developed angioedema (swelling) 20 to 30 minutes after a meal that contained oregano; an oral food challenge with oregano was positive. A 1996 case report describes three systemic allergic reactions caused by eating oregano (Origanum vulgare) and thyme in one patient, who had specific IgE to all the mint-family herbs tested; the abstract does not describe the reactions or say which herb caused each one. A 2025 review of spice and herb allergy in children names oregano among the commonly implicated herbs and says symptoms range from mild oral reactions to anaphylaxis; the abstract does not say which reactions oregano caused. Oregano oil: a 2020 record is titled 'Irritant contact dermatitis after a curious therapeutic use of oregano essential oil'; it has no abstract, so it supports only its title. In a 2022 randomized trial in 34 trained athletes, 14 days of essential oil from one of two oregano species (Origanum dubium or Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum; a third group received lavender oil) left liver biomarkers no different from a control group; the abstract does not give the route or report adverse events, and no trial adverse-event data for oregano oil taken by mouth were found in the cited sources. Interactions: acenocoumarol (one case report) is the only medicine named in the cited sources.
